answer: I'd like to talk about something I borrowed last year that turned out to be a great help. Something I once borrowed that proved incredibly useful was a professional camera I borrowed from a close friend for a family event. The event was a small gathering we held at home when my father retired after running his business for over thirty years. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her family, and my grandparents travelled in from the village, so I knew it was a day worth remembering. I had wanted to capture the occasion properly but could not justify buying an expensive camera for a single day. My friend, who is a keen photographer, generously offered to lend me his, which was very [[considerate]] of him. I was slightly nervous about handling such a valuable and [[delicate]] piece of equipment. He kindly gave me a quick lesson on how to use it, which I really appreciated. The photos it produced were of a quality I could never have achieved with my phone, so I was genuinely [[grateful]]. My favourite is a shot of my father laughing with my grandfather, which now sits framed in our living room. I made sure to return it promptly and in perfect condition, as I did not want to [[betray his trust]]. I also printed a few of the best photos for him as a small thank-you. Honestly, the whole experience reminded me how valuable it is to have [[generous]] friends. It also made me consider eventually investing in a decent camera of my own.

followUps.q: Do you often borrow things from others?
followUps.answer: Not often. I don't like troubling people, so I only borrow when it's really necessary, and I always make sure I return things quickly and in the same condition.

followUps.q: Do you lend your own things to friends?
followUps.answer: Yes, usually books. I'm happy to lend them, although I've learnt to write my name inside the cover, because a few have [[mysteriously vanished]] over the years.

note: Made the family event his father's retirement gathering with the whole family present; added the favourite photo and thank-you gesture; new mark 'betray his trust'.
